paras: The lynching of Jim Winget was the hanging of a Black man, Jim Winget, also known as Jim Cason, by unidentified men in Bossier Parish, Louisiana, on a Tuesday night in mid-August 1890. Winget was taken from his house and hanged in a yard a mile and a half away, and he was said to have been a witness in a pending murder case. The killing is known from a single short paragraph in the Shreveport Caucasian, reprinted in the Bossier Banner.

At the time, N. H. Wyche was accused of killing a young man near Plain Dealing in Bossier Parish. In the same issue that carried the lynching report, the Bossier Banner noted that Governor Nicholls had offered a $250 reward for the apprehension of Nat H. Wyche, "who murdered W. R. Hollman, in this parish, on July 9, 1890." According to the Caucasian, Winget was a witness in the Wyche case, and it was "also stated" that he "was indirectly connected in the homicide."

On Tuesday night, by the Caucasian's account, "parties unknown" took Winget from his house on the H. D. Kelly place. They carried him a mile and a half and hanged him in "Wyche's yard." The paper presented his role in the murder case as hearsay but called the seizure and hanging "a fact."
No report of an inquest, arrest or investigation into Winget's death appears in the coverage.

The Shreveport Caucasian printed the item on August 15 on the word of "a reliable gentleman," and the Bossier Banner reprinted it on August 21 under the headline "A NEGRO LYNCHED." The Banner offered no comment on the lynchers, and its reward notice for Wyche that week did not mention Winget. No other white paper's report of the lynching and no Black-press coverage were found.

The two items in the Banner name the victim of the related homicide differently: the Caucasian called him "a young man named Smith," while the governor's reward notice named W. R. Hollman. The reward notice is the more formal source; the Caucasian's came secondhand from an informant.

reader.title: Lynching of Jim Winget
bases: The Shreveport Caucasian, reprinted in the Bossier Banner, reported that Winget was taken from his house by 'parties unknown' at night and hanged a mile and a half away [A1].

Winget was taken from his home and hanged by 'parties unknown' with no lawful authority, and the paper called it a lynching [A1]; the number of men is not given, and the only hint of motive is that he was a witness in, and was 'stated' to be 'indirectly connected' with, a pending murder case [A1].
The only account is one Shreveport Caucasian paragraph, itself based on a 'reliable gentleman', reprinted in the Bossier Banner [A1]; no other paper's report was found.

No town given for the lynching; it took place between the H. D. Kelly place and Wyche's yard in Bossier Parish. The related homicide was near Plain Dealing.
